name: Omar Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a line crew for the power company out on the industrial corridor east of town, where they're building warehouses, a battery plant and two big solar farms. So my days are mostly new feeders, tying those solar farms into the grid, setting switches, and the odd emergency when a contractor digs through a cable. I'm in the truck by six-thirty and I plan the day on my phone with an AI assistant before the crew turns up. I love the building side, watching an empty field turn into something that powers a thousand homes. What wears me out is waiting on other people's permits.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Samira is a pharmacist, we've got a boy who's twelve and a girl who's eight, and a mortgage on a house near the mosque on Elm Street. On weekends my brother-in-law Yusuf and I run a small solar and EV-charger installation business, and we co-own the little workshop unit it runs from. I use AI every day, for quotes, for wiring calcs, even to draft the invoices. My father drove a taxi for thirty years, and he always said, 'Work for yourself if you can,' so the side business is me listening to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, nothing more, and the people who used it well still came out ahead. I'd say keep working hard, the basics don't change. At the mosque and with the crew, nobody would be shocked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, even good. I keep the edge it gives me on quotes, and the line work stays the same. The side business keeps growing because people still want solar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing both jobs, keep using the tools, and keep growing the weekend business. Yusuf and I would probably hire our first part-time helper this year. And keep paying down the mortgage on schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Business as usual, which suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the AI actually save you on quotes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quote used to take me most of a Sunday evening. Now it's forty minutes, and it's more accurate. That's an extra evening a week with my kids, which is worth more to me than any robot they could build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it hard doing two jobs with young kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some weeks, yes. Samira keeps me honest, she'll say 'no jobs this Saturday, it's your daughter's recital.' Family first, then work, then the business.

S0.say: It's a good tool and nothing more, and the people who used it well still came out ahead. Keep working hard, because the basics don't change.
S0.think: For me it's fine, even good: I keep the edge it gives me on quotes, and the line work stays the same. The side business keeps growing because people still want solar.
S0.do: Keeps working both jobs and growing the weekend solar business, likely hiring a first part-time helper this year. Keeps paying down the mortgage on schedule.
S0.feel: Calm; business as usual suits him.
S0.quote: That's an extra evening a week with my kids, which is worth more to me than any robot they could build.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is energetic, enterprising and family-minded, carrying his taxi-driver father's advice to work for himself. He uses AI to win back time with his children. His wife sets the boundaries around work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people willing to work and learn. The market will reward the ones who adapt. I'd tell young guys to learn a trade and the tools, not wait for the government to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. Line work isn't going anywhere fast, and the side business could use AI and some automation to scale up. The big risk is that bigger companies do the same thing cheaper and squeeze out small outfits like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invest in better software for the side business, maybe a drone for roof surveys, and use AI to handle scheduling. I'd hire one or two part-timers and make the business a real company. At the power company, I'd volunteer my crew for any robot or drone trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bigger companies might squeeze you out. How would you compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Service and trust. The big national firms send a different guy every time and nobody answers the phone. Half my customers found me at Friday prayers, and no app is going to beat that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the power company for the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. The power company pays well, there's a pension, and the kids are young. Maybe in five or ten years, once the business is bigger and steadier.

S1.say: This is a chance for people willing to work and learn, and the market will reward those who adapt. I'd tell young guys to learn a trade and the tools rather than wait for the government.
S1.think: It's good for me, because line work isn't going anywhere fast and the side business could use AI and automation to scale up. The risk is bigger companies doing the same cheaper and squeezing out small outfits like ours.
S1.do: Invests in better software and a roof-survey drone for the side business and uses AI for scheduling. Hires one or two part-timers to make it a real company and volunteers his crew for robot and drone trials.
S1.quote: Half my customers found me at Friday prayers, and no app is going to beat that.
S1.fieldNote: Omar sees gradual disruption as an opening, especially for his side business. His free-market views come with a realistic fear of bigger competitors. His community ties are his competitive edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be rough, and people need to lean on family and community and get busy, not sit and wait for handouts. Businesses that move fast will survive. I'd still be saying adapt or get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years would rattle me more than I'd say. If robots can do line work and install solar panels by 2028, both my jobs are in play. I've got savings, the workshop and Samira's job, so we wouldn't go hungry, but I'd be scrambling to figure out where the money is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, Yusuf and I would sit down and look at buying robot installers ourselves rather than competing with them. I'd move some savings into the business for that and keep the rest safe for the mortgage. At the power company, I'd ask to run their robot crews, since I already know the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of adrenaline. More like a race than a fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both jobs are in play. Which one would you fight for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The business, because it's ours. The power company decides for me; with the business, I decide. If a robot is going to install solar panels in my town, I'd rather it had my name on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Samira say about putting savings into robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say show me the numbers first, which is fair. She's careful, I'm the risk taker. We'd agree on a limit, maybe a third of the savings, and not a cent more.

S2.say: This will be rough, and people need to lean on family and community and get busy rather than wait for handouts. Businesses that move fast will survive, so adapt or get left behind.
S2.think: Two years would rattle me more than I'd say, because both my jobs are in play if robots can do line work and install panels. We wouldn't go hungry, but I'd be scrambling to find where the money is.
S2.do: Looks with his brother-in-law at buying robot installers rather than competing with them, moving up to a third of savings into the business. Asks the power company to let him run its robot crews.
S2.feel: Uneasy but full of adrenaline, more like a race than a fear.
S2.quote: If a robot is going to install solar panels in my town, I'd rather it had my name on the side.
S2.fieldNote: Omar's response to the fastest scenario is to buy into automation rather than resist it. His strong cushion, his wife's income and his comfort with risk keep him in race mode rather than fear. His wife's caution acts as a brake, and he respects it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good window for anyone willing to work. Learn the new tools, start something on the side, look after your family. I'd tell people not to wait for the government to save them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is just right for me. I'd have time to grow the business, buy into the robot installers early, and keep my line job while it lasts. I think I'd come out better off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd register the business properly, hire two people and buy our first robot-assisted installation kit once a couple of reviews say it works. I'd learn everything I could about running robot crews at the power company. We'd also start a savings fund for the kids' education.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, almost hungry for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'not wait for the government.' What about people who can't do what you can?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family and community first, then help from the government if they really need it. I'm not heartless. But I've seen people wait for help that never came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn how things work, wires and code. I'd tell him the robot is just a very expensive apprentice, and somebody still has to be the boss.

S3.say: Five years is a good window for anyone willing to work: learn the new tools, start something on the side and look after your family. Don't wait for the government to save you.
S3.think: Five years is just right for me, with time to grow the business, buy into robot installers early and keep my line job while it lasts. I think I'd come out better off.
S3.do: Registers the business properly, hires two people and buys a robot-assisted installation kit once reviews confirm it works. Learns to run robot crews at the power company and starts an education fund for the children.
S3.quote: I'd tell him the robot is just a very expensive apprentice, and somebody still has to be the boss.
S3.fieldNote: Five years puts Omar firmly in opportunity mode; he expects to come out ahead. His free-market view softens slightly when pressed, accepting government help as a last resort. His 'expensive apprentice' line sums up his attitude to robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone who wants to adapt. Start now, learn the tools, save money, and build something. I'd say it to the crew, to my friends, everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is great. I'd be fifty-three with a real business and maybe I'd have left the power company by then. My worry is getting comfortable and letting the big firms get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the business steadily, add EV chargers and battery systems, and slowly bring in robots as they get cheaper. I'd stay at the power company for a few years, then maybe go full-time on the business around year five. Keep paying off the house and saving for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you go full-time on the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When it makes as much as my line job for two years in a row. Samira and I agreed on that rule already. I don't jump until the business has paid my salary twice; that's my wife's rule and it's a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you uneasy over the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, mostly, and maybe the kids' generation not learning to work with their hands. But I've got time, savings and a good partner. I'm not losing sleep.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty for anyone who wants to adapt, so start now, learn the tools, save money and build something. I'd say it to the crew, my friends, everyone.
S4.think: Ten years is great for me, since at fifty-three I'd have a real business and may have left the power company. My worry is getting comfortable and letting the big firms get ahead.
S4.do: Grows the business steadily, adds EV chargers and battery systems, and brings in robots as they get cheaper. Stays at the power company for a few years, then considers going full-time on the business around year five while paying off the house and saving for the children.
S4.quote: I don't jump until the business has paid my salary twice; that's my wife's rule and it's a good one.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Omar is relaxed and confident, with a clear rule agreed with his wife for when to leave his job. His only worries are bigger competitors and his children's generation losing hands-on skills. His approach blends free-market ambition with family caution.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit both my jobs at once, before the business was big enough to carry us. What would help is small businesses getting a fair chance to buy the robots too, not just the big firms, and banks willing to lend to people like me who want to build something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the robots. Everyone asks if a robot will take my job, but the real question is whether a guy like me can ever own one. That's what decides if this is good or bad for working people.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if a robot will take my job, but the real question is whether a guy like me can ever own one.
portrait: Omar Khan is a 43-year-old line crew lead on a growing industrial corridor, connecting solar farms and factories, who also runs a weekend solar and EV-charger business with his brother-in-law. He's married to a pharmacist, has two children and a mortgage, and uses AI every day for planning and quotes. He's calm across the slower scenarios and sees them as openings for his business, and only uneasy, in a racing rather than fearful way, when AGI arrives in two years. His answer to every scenario is to own the automation rather than fight it, while his wife's caution keeps him grounded. He believes in hard work, family and community first, with government as a last resort.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would hit both his jobs at once before the business could carry the family.
whatWouldHelp: Small businesses getting a fair chance to buy robots, not just big firms, and banks willing to lend to people who want to build something.
